Can a squatter become the owner of a Pennsylvania house?

Yes, but only by meeting a demanding statute over many years and then winning a court judgment. Pennsylvania has no automatic transfer of title to a person who simply lives in or uses a property.

The shorter route is 42 Pa.C.S. 5527.1, which allows title after at least 10 years of actual, continuous, exclusive, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile possession. The longer background rule is in 42 Pa.C.S. 5530(a)(1): an action for possession of real property must be commenced within 21 years, except as section 5527.1 provides.

Property the 10-year claim can reach

Section 5527.1 defines the property narrowly. Under subsection (h), the claim covers real estate of no more than one-half acre that meets both of these tests.

  • It is improved by a single-family dwelling that the possessor has occupied for the full 10 years.
  • It appears as a separate lot in a recorded conveyance, subdivision plan or official municipal map or plan.

A possessor may add an abutting contiguous lot that has been regularly used as part of the property, as long as the two together stay within one-half acre and the possessor has held the lot with the same hostile possession for 10 years. The section does not apply to condominiums, cooperatives or planned communities, or to land owned by the United States, the Commonwealth, a local government, an authority or a school district.

Steps a possessor must take in court

The possessor must file a quiet title action and give notice to the record owners, their heirs, successors and assigns. The notice has to use a form approved by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. It must carry the metes and bounds description, the deed reference, the street address, the zip code, the parcel number and a statement of the one-year period to respond.

Owners then have one year to file an ejectment action disputing the claim. If they file, serve it and win, both the 10-year and the 21-year limitation periods are tolled and the court enters judgment for the owners. If nobody files within the year, the court may enter judgment granting title by adverse possession.

Does stepping onto the land stop the clock?

Not by itself. Under 42 Pa.C.S. 5530(b), an owner's entry on the property does not toll the 21-year period unless a possessory action is commenced within one year after the entry. Repeat attempts follow the same rule: an entry and possessory action that ends without recovery does not toll the period for another possessory action unless that other action starts within one year after the first one ends.

A visit to the property, a locked gate or a verbal warning does not protect an owner's title. A filed lawsuit does, and it has to follow the entry quickly. Owners of vacant houses, inherited property and rental units that sit empty should check them on a schedule and write down what they find.

Time limits side by side

Several clocks run in these cases, and each depends on the route.

Time limits in 42 Pa.C.S. 5527.1 and 5530
RulePeriodWhat it governs
Section 5527.1(a)10 yearsPossession needed to acquire title to qualifying property
Section 5527.1(d)1 yearOwner's window to file ejectment after notice
Section 5530(a)(1)21 yearsTime to commence an action for possession of real property
Section 5530(b)1 year after entryEntry on land tolls the period only if a possessory action follows within a year

If the owners win the ejectment case, any later claim based on adverse possession starts counting no earlier than the date of that judgment.

Liens and mortgages after a judgment

A judgment granting title by adverse possession does not by itself discharge easements, profits, covenants, mortgages, liens, judgments or leases that run with the title. It does not extend or shorten the time in which claims against the property may be asserted, and it does not override the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code or local zoning and land use ordinances.

The remedy is nonexclusive, so a possessor may also have other routes, including a determination of title to a decedent's interest under 20 Pa.C.S. 3546.

How an owner can remove an unwanted occupant

The civil tools are ejectment and, in some situations, a quiet title action. Rule 1051 says an ejectment case follows the ordinary rules for a civil action. Rule 1061(b) lists the purposes of a quiet title action, including compelling an adverse party to commence an ejectment action and obtaining possession of land sold at a judicial or tax sale.

Both the 21-year clock and the 10-year clock run against the owner, so a written notice or an early complaint can matter. Act before a possessor's notice reaches you, and talk to a Pennsylvania real estate attorney as soon as you learn someone is living in a vacant house.

Is entering someone's property a crime?

It can be, depending on how the person got in and what the owner told them. Criminal trespass under 18 Pa.C.S. 3503 has several levels.

  • Entering a building or occupied structure, or surreptitiously remaining in it, knowing you have no license or privilege, is a felony of the third degree.
  • Breaking into a building or occupied structure is a felony of the second degree.
  • A defiant trespasser who ignores notice against trespass commits at least a summary offense, and a misdemeanor of the third degree if the person defies an order to leave that the owner or an authorized person communicated personally.

Defenses exist, including that the building was abandoned and that the actor reasonably believed the owner would have allowed entry. Keep written proof that you own the house and that you told the occupant to leave.

Selling a house that has an occupant

Settle who has the right to be there before you list. A buyer or closing agent reviewing title will ask whether anyone claims an interest, and a pending quiet title or ejectment case can complicate that review.

  • Check the recorded deed and the tax records for your county.
  • Keep dated records of any visits, repairs and tax payments, since the possession tests turn on use over time.
  • Write to the occupant and keep proof of delivery.
  • Ask a Pennsylvania attorney whether ejectment is the right first step.

Once the occupancy question is settled, a buyer can see clearly what is being bought. A cash buyer will still want the same answers, so expect the title company to ask for them.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Pennsylvania?

At least 10 years of qualifying possession for a single-family house on a lot of one-half acre or less. The general limit for an action to recover real property is 21 years.

Do squatters have rights to a vacant house?

No automatic rights. A possessor must meet every element of section 5527.1, file a quiet title action and give notice, and a court enters judgment only if owners do not respond within one year.

Can paying property taxes help an adverse possession claim?

Section 5527.1 lists no tax element. Its required elements are actual, continuous, exclusive, visible, notorious, distinct and hostile possession. Ask an attorney how a court would weigh tax payments.

Does the 10-year rule apply to condominiums or government land?

No. Section 5527.1 does not apply to condominiums, cooperatives or planned communities, or to land owned by federal, state or local government bodies.

What if the owner files for ejectment in time?

If the owners file and serve an ejectment action within the one-year notice period and win, the 10-year and 21-year limitation periods are tolled and the court enters judgment in the owners' favor.

Laws that cover a rented house

Several statutes apply at once. A landlord planning to sell should know all of them, because each one sets duties owed to the tenant while the house is still rented. The Office of Attorney General's consumer guide for tenants and landlords lists these.

Laws that apply to Pennsylvania residential rentals
LawWhat it covers
Landlord and Tenant Act, 68 P.S. 250.101 to 250.60Basic leasing rules, deposits, notices to quit
Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, 73 P.S. 201-1 to 201-9.2Deceptive rental practices
Responsible Utility Customer Protection Act, 66 Pa.C.S. 1401 to 1419Utility shutoff notices
Utility Service Tenant Rights Act, 68 P.S. 399.1 to 399.19aTenant remedies when a landlord stops paying a utility
Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, 43 P.S. 951 to 963Housing discrimination
Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. 3601 to 3631Housing discrimination

Philadelphia adds Philadelphia Code chapters 9-800 and 9-1100, and Pittsburgh has its own code provisions. City rules can go beyond the state floor, so a landlord with a house inside either city should read the local code too.

How tenancies and lease terms carry over to a new owner

Two arrangements are common: a fixed-period lease, and a periodic tenancy that repeats month to month or year to year. A lease of three years or less may be oral or written. A longer lease must be written. A periodic tenancy renews on its own unless one side gives at least 15 days' notice before the current term ends, under 68 P.S. 250.501(b).

Rent and other terms generally cannot change until renewal unless both parties agree in writing, so a sale does not rewrite the lease. Clauses that violate the law are unenforceable. Examples include clauses that make the tenant accept the unit as is, take over all maintenance and repairs, or give up a hearing.

Before you market a rental, gather every signed or written term. A buyer will ask for them, and an investor buyer will want to see exactly what the tenant is paying and until when.

  • Written lease, any length: copy it for the buyer.
  • Oral lease of three years or less: write down the rent, the due date and the start date.
  • Month to month: note when the current term ends.

Fair housing rules for landlords

The state Human Relations Act and the federal Fair Housing Act bar discrimination in renting based on race, color, religious creed, ancestry, age of forty and older, sex, pregnancy or childbirth, national origin, familial status, disability, and use of a guide animal because of blindness or deafness. Prohibited conduct includes discriminatory advertising, different fees or terms, falsely saying a unit is unavailable, and refusing reasonable modifications or accommodations for a person with a disability.

There are limits. The state act does not apply to owner-occupied buildings with two units. The federal act does not apply to owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units, to single-family houses rented by an owner without an agent, or to housing run by religious organizations and private clubs that limit occupancy to members. A landlord selling a duplex they live in stands differently from one who owns a rented house across town.

On screening, a landlord must disclose when a credit or tenant screening report led to a denial, and the applicant may request a free copy within 60 days. Philadelphia bars refusing a tenant only because of an eviction record or a credit score under a set number. Landlords elsewhere in the state are encouraged to follow the same approach.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Pennsylvania house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Repairs, access and utilities

Every lease carries an implied warranty of habitability. Failures include lost heat in winter, no hot or cold running water, rodent infestation, a leaking roof, unsafe floors or stairs and broken locks. A lease clause cannot waive the duty. Tenants are told to notify the landlord, allow a reasonable time, document everything and get legal advice before using a remedy.

Utilities run on their own timetable. Under the Responsible Utility Customer Protection Act, a utility must give written notice ten days before a shutoff and attempt contact three days before. From December through March it must also post a notice 48 hours before. If a landlord fails to pay for service, the Utility Service Tenant Rights Act requires at least 30 days' notice to tenants, who may then pay the utility and deduct those payments from rent.

Settle utility accounts for rented units before you list. An unpaid bill can hand the tenant a remedy, and it can surface in a buyer's inspection period as a problem.

Leaving early and retaliation

No stand-alone right to end a lease early exists, and many leases do not allow it. A tenant who moves out with no breach by the landlord will probably owe rent until the lease expires or the landlord re-rents the unit. The landlord has no duty to find a replacement.

Retaliation is less clear. No general state law bars a landlord from retaliating against tenants for using their landlord-tenant rights, though cities and townships may have ordinances, and Philadelphia does. The Utility Service Tenant Rights Act protects tenants who pay a utility and deduct it, and the discrimination laws protect people who complain or take part in a housing proceeding. A landlord cannot end or refuse to renew a lease because a tenant joined a tenants' organization, under 68 P.S. 250.205.

What happens after an eviction judgment?

The sequence starts with a written Notice to Quit: ten days for unpaid rent or illegal drugs, and fifteen or thirty days for other breaches depending on the lease length. If the tenant stays, the landlord files with the Magisterial District Court, the Philadelphia Municipal Court or the Allegheny County Housing Court. Self-help is not allowed. Locks and utilities stay untouched until a court order is carried out.

Two details matter to an owner who plans to sell. First, when an eviction is only for unpaid rent, the tenant can stop it by paying the full unpaid rent and fees at any point before the actual eviction, under 246 Pa. Code 518. The landlord must then have the court mark the judgment satisfied. If a written request goes unanswered for 90 days without good cause, the landlord owes the tenant 1 percent of the judgment each month, with a floor of $250 and a ceiling of $2,500, under 42 Pa.C.S. 8104(b).

Second, Pennsylvania does not automatically seal or expunge eviction records, even for a withdrawn case.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pennsylvania houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Free legal help

Tenants may file a landlord-tenant complaint with the Attorney General's Bureau of Consumer Protection, a civil rights complaint with the Civil Rights Enforcement Section, or a utility complaint with the Office of Consumer Advocate. Discrimination complaints go to the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission or to HUD.

  • Community Legal Services serves low-income residents of Philadelphia.
  • Neighborhood Legal Services covers Allegheny, Beaver, Butler and Lawrence counties.
  • MidPenn Legal Services covers a band of counties across south central Pennsylvania, including Dauphin, Lancaster and York.
  • Northwestern Legal Services covers Erie, Mercer and several other northwestern counties.
  • The Pennsylvania Bar Association runs a lawyer referral service in most counties.

A landlord with a rental to sell can use the same referral channels to find an attorney who handles tenant matters before the listing goes up.

Frequently asked questions

Does selling the house cancel my tenant's lease?

No. Rent and other terms generally cannot change until renewal unless both sides agree in writing, so a sale does not rewrite them. Have a Pennsylvania attorney check how your specific lease treats a transfer.

Can a landlord enter a rented unit to show it?

A tenant must allow reasonable access for maintenance, repairs and showing the unit to a future tenant. Showings to a buyer are a separate matter, so set times with the tenant in writing.

Can an eviction be stopped after judgment for unpaid rent?

Yes, if the eviction is only for unpaid rent. The tenant can pay the full unpaid rent and fees at any point before the actual eviction under 246 Pa. Code 518.

Does Pennsylvania erase an eviction record?

No. The state does not automatically seal or expunge eviction records, even if the case was withdrawn. A record can look unpaid if the landlord never has the judgment marked satisfied.

Where do I report a landlord who ignores a defect?

A tenant can file a complaint with the Bureau of Consumer Protection at the Office of Attorney General. The tenant should also document the problem and consult a lawyer before withholding rent.

title: Pennsylvania Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Pennsylvania Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Pennsylvania Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Pennsylvania Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Pennsylvania House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Pennsylvania?

Written notice before a Pennsylvania eviction

A landlord must start with a written Notice to Quit, and the length of that notice turns on the reason for ending the tenancy. The time periods come from the Landlord and Tenant Act, 68 P.S. 250.501(b) and 250.505-A.

The notice does not end the tenancy by itself. It starts a clock, and if the tenant is still in the house when the clock runs out, the landlord has to go to court for possession. Changing locks or removing belongings is not part of the lawful process.

Notice to Quit periods by reason for eviction
ReasonDays to leave voluntarily
Failure to pay rent10
Use of illegal drugs10
Other lease breach, lease of one year or less or indeterminate term15
Other lease breach, lease longer than one year30

How a Notice to Quit is delivered, and lease waivers

Under 68 P.S. 250.501(f), the landlord can give the notice to the tenant in person, leave it at the main building of the leased property, or post it conspicuously on the property.

A lease can waive the notice. Waiver of notice to quit clauses are common, and if one is valid, the landlord may file a complaint in court with no advance notice at all. The Attorney General's office encourages landlords not to include such clauses, but the law permits them. Read the lease for a waiver clause before relying on the day counts above.

  • Month-to-month and year-to-year tenancies renew automatically unless one side gives at least 15 days' notice before the current month or year ends.
  • A lease of three years or less can be oral or written, and a lease for more than three years must be in writing.

After the notice period ends

The landlord files a Landlord-Tenant Complaint. That filing goes to the Magisterial District Court for the county, to the Philadelphia Municipal Court in Philadelphia, or to the Housing Court in Allegheny County. The complaint asks for possession and may also ask for back rent or damages.

The court issues a summons with a hearing date, mails it to the tenant's last known address by first-class mail, and has a sheriff or certified constable serve it in person or by posting. A tenant with a claim against the landlord, such as a breach of the implied warranty of habitability, must file a counterclaim before the hearing date. A tenant who misses the hearing loses by default.

Each court follows its own local rules, so look up the rules for the court named on the summons before the hearing date arrives.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Pennsylvania house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The hearing and the appeal

At the hearing each side presents its case, and the judge issues a Notice of Judgment at the end of the hearing or within three days. If the landlord wins, the landlord is granted possession and the judge may also award unpaid rent and damages.

A tenant who loses has 10 days after entry of judgment to appeal to the court of common pleas. The appeal stops an actual eviction only if the tenant deposits with the court the lesser of three months' rent or the amount the judge ordered paid. A low-income tenant can file an affidavit and deposit one third of a month's rent, and in both cases monthly rent must keep being deposited while the appeal is pending. A survivor of domestic violence has 30 days to appeal under 68 P.S. 250.513(b).

When a tenant can actually be removed

Only after an order of possession, and the landlord cannot request it until 10 days after the judgment. The court mails the order and a sheriff or certified constable serves it personally or by posting. The order requires the tenant to vacate within 10 days of service, and on the 11th day after service the tenant can be forcibly evicted.

  • If belongings are left behind after a forced eviction, the landlord must mail notice of the right to retrieve them by first-class mail.
  • The tenant then has 10 days from the postmark to pick them up or ask the landlord to store them, for up to 30 days at the tenant's cost.
  • In a nonpayment case the tenant can stop the eviction at any point before it happens by paying all unpaid rent and fees.

After a payment, the landlord should record the judgment as satisfied. If the landlord fails to do so within 90 days of a written request, the landlord can owe 1 percent of the judgment each month, with a floor of $250 and a ceiling of $2,500.

Local programs and court rules that can pause a case

Local courts set their own procedures, so check the local rules of the court where the complaint was filed. The Philadelphia Municipal Court, for example, continues a hearing when the tenant has a complaint accepted by the Philadelphia Fair Housing Commission before the date the landlord filed for eviction.

Some cities, Philadelphia among them, may offer eviction diversion or mediation programs that help the parties reach an agreement without a full court process or an eviction record. Do not assume one exists in a given county. Ask the court clerk or the county lawyer referral service what is offered.

  • Tenants can ask the court to reschedule a hearing they cannot attend, but they should contact the court before the date.
  • Tenants can bring a lawyer, documents, photos, emails and records to the hearing.
  • Landlords pursuing both possession and rent can ask for both in a single complaint.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pennsylvania houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How an eviction affects selling a Pennsylvania house

An owner planning to sell a tenant-occupied house should keep the notice, the complaint, the judgment and the order of possession together in one file. Each document shows where the case stands, and anyone reviewing the property will ask for them.

Pennsylvania does not automatically seal or expunge eviction records, even when a case is withdrawn, and a judgment can still appear unsatisfied if the landlord never filed the satisfaction. After any payment, make sure the court record is updated. Ask the court clerk for the docket and a lawyer or lawyer referral service for advice on timing.

A buyer usually wants the house delivered empty, so the sale timeline follows the eviction timeline. A cash buyer who purchases as-is can take on repairs and cleanup, but possession still has to be delivered lawfully at closing.

Frequently asked questions

How many days is a Pennsylvania eviction notice?

Ten days for unpaid rent or illegal drug use, 15 days for another breach under a lease of one year or less, and 30 days for another breach under a lease longer than one year. These periods come from 68 P.S. 250.501(b).

Can a Pennsylvania landlord evict without a court order?

No, the landlord must file a complaint, win a judgment, wait 10 days, and obtain an order of possession served by a sheriff or certified constable. Even then, forcible removal can happen only on the 11th day after service of that order, and the landlord may not act alone.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent owed?

Yes, when the eviction is only for failure to pay rent, paying the full unpaid rent and fees before the actual eviction stops it. The landlord should then enter satisfaction of the judgment with the court.

How long does a tenant have to appeal?

Ten days after judgment is entered, with an appeal to the court of common pleas. A survivor of domestic violence has 30 days, and the appeal blocks removal only if the required deposit is made.

Where is the eviction complaint filed?

In the county's Magisterial District Court, except that Philadelphia uses the Municipal Court and Allegheny County uses the Housing Court. The same court issues the summons and the order of possession.
